entries.answer: A weekend is the first free stretch most people get, and the reason plans for it fail is usually that they were made for a version of the person who has more energy than they do. A plan that works is built around one anchor and left loose around it: one thing that takes the morning, a long gap, and nothing after dinner. The anchor should be chosen by weather rather than mood, since a rained-on outdoor plan is the one that gets abandoned, and an indoor one with a walk attached survives a bad day. If the weekend is a Sunday only, the pressure to make it count is higher than it should be, because Sunday is the last day before the week restarts and most of it is spent preparing for it. The most reliable Sunday is one with a single slow morning and a small errand that gets you out of the house, and a person who is tired will be glad of the errand rather than seeing it as a failure to rest.

entries.answer: A lazy day is a real and useful plan rather than a failure to have one, and the reason it needs defending is that a free day gets filled by default. The gap in a day is normally taken by a phone, and an afternoon of that leaves a person tired in a way an afternoon outside does not. What makes a day genuinely restful is doing something with a clear end and no evaluation: a whole film, a bath, cooking something that takes an hour, a walk with no destination. The failure mode is deciding the day must be productive and then feeling worse by evening, which is a worse outcome than doing nothing at all. In the Philippines the weather makes this easier since most of the year it is warm enough to sit outside, and an evening with a barangay or a friend is not an event but the ordinary shape of a day off.

entries.answer: Sobrang init is the Tagalog remark for it being very hot, and it is one of the most ordinary things a Filipino says, because in the Philippines the heat is a shared condition rather than a personal one. The phrase is a superlative built from sobra, meaning too much or very, and the same form covers the other end with lamig, so a person moves between sobrang init and sobrang lamig depending on the month. Init also means heat generally, so init ng araw is the heat of the sun and maalapan na ang araw means the day is getting late, which is a different sense people confuse. Practical advice in the heat is mostly ordinary: water, lighter clothing, and not doing the outside work in the afternoon, since the sun in the Philippines is strongest well before the middle of the day. A person who mentions the heat is usually about to explain why they cannot do something, so the remark is rarely only about the weather.
